hits.draft_en:
Pieter Levels and Steve Lacey both noticed it: given the choice, AI agents almost never use MCP servers. 92k views, 263 bookmarks.

Steve's explanation is practical. An MCP connector needs a human to install and configure it first. An API key in a .env file or a browser is already there, so the agent just uses that.

If you're building for agents, make the first step something the agent can do on its own.
hits.video_tip: 12s: split screen, an agent stuck on 'please install the connector' versus the same agent calling the API with a key from .env and finishing, caption 'agents take the path with no human step'.

outsiders.name: Steve Lacey 🔥
outsiders.text:
I build MCP into my apps. My own agents almost never use it.

My setup is simple. Each agent is a Claude Code session with its own project folder and a .env containing whatever keys it needs. I tell it to get something done. I don’t care how.

It almost never picks MCP.

Not because MCP is bad, but because of the connector step. In most setups, a human has to install and configure the connector before the agent can use it. The agent can’t do that part, so it stops and asks me to get up, go to the computer and click things.

Meanwhile, it could just call the API or open a browser. So that’s what it does.

I’ve had agents quietly work around MCP servers that I’d built specifically for them, only to discover afterwards that they’d never used them.

This also breaks the thing everyone seems to be doing right now: the “copy this prompt to get started” button.

I assumed the point of that prompt was to tell the agent how to use your MCP. But it can’t. Someone pastes it into a regular ChatGPT conversation, and the first thing it does is tell them to go install a connector.

Most people are gone at that point.

So the prompt has to lead with full instructions for operating without your MCP. Which rather defeats the point.

I suspect the connector step eventually dies. Agents should be able to just use these things. Configure yourself, robot.

But here’s why I’m still building MCP.

The whole point of an API contract is to stop the code consuming your API from breaking. You version it, deprecate things slowly, maintain backwards compatibility and support old endpoints for years, because somebody’s code depends on them staying exactly the same.

With an agent, there’s no consuming code to maintain. It reads your documentation in seconds, works out what’s available today and gets on with it. It doesn’t care what the API looked like yesterday.

That means you can rewrite the whole thing whenever you like. You can expose capabilities you’d never bother putting in a conventional API: creating an account, changing a profile picture, deleting an account. The agent picks up the latest instructions every time.

That’s the part of MCP I think survives.

Not connectors. Not directories. Not the installation dance.

Just this:

MCP ends up meaning “API without a contract.”

And that’s a good thing.

virals.angle: Agents skip MCP when there's a human step
virals.draft_en:
Pieter Levels and Steve Lacey noticed the same thing this week: given the choice, AI agents almost never use MCP servers.

Steve's reason is simple. An MCP connector usually needs a human to install and configure it. An API key in .env, or a browser, is already there. So the agent takes the path with no human step. He's even found agents quietly working around MCP servers he built for them.

If you're building for agents:
1. Make setup something the agent can do itself
2. Offer a plain API next to any MCP
3. Check your logs to see which path agents actually use
virals.inspired_by: @levelsio MCP take (92k, 263 bookmarks) + @stevelacey 'my own agents almost never use it' (87k) + @rauchg agents need their workspace (28k)
virals.video_tip: 12s: split screen, agent paused on 'please install the connector' versus the same agent calling the API and finishing, caption 'agents take the path with no human step'.

virals.angle: Price the agent job before you start
virals.draft_en:
Pieter Levels decompiled Battlefield 1942 and put it in the browser with multiplayer. 162k views, 860 bookmarks.

The useful number came after: about 1 million output tokens, roughly $100 at API prices, covered by his $100/month Claude plan.

That gives you a rule of thumb. A serious weekend agent project can eat about a month of a plan. Before a big run, estimate tokens, compare against your plan and API price, and decide which one to use.
virals.inspired_by: @levelsio BF1942 on the web (162k, 860 bookmarks) + 1M tokens about $100 (50k) + @theo hit his $200 Muse limit (64k) + @tdinh_me 'need more tokens' (6k)
virals.video_tip: 10s: the game running in a tab, then a cost card '1M output tokens = ~$100 API = 1 month plan', caption 'do the token math first'.

virals.angle: Sell the agent like an employee
virals.draft_en:
Greg Isenberg's most-saved post this week (2.6k bookmarks): set up Grok Bots for boring businesses. Give each agent its own computer, email and phone number, and charge like you're hiring an employee for $12 an hour.

The reason it works: small business owners already know how to buy labor. They don't want to learn software.

Start small. Pick one repetitive job at one local business, run it for two weeks, count the hours saved, and price against that number.
virals.inspired_by: @gregisenberg Grok Bots for SMBs (125k, 2.6k bookmarks) + @AlexFinn team of agents for $200 (36k) + @elonmusk 'treat Bot like a colleague' (820k)
virals.video_tip: 12s: whiteboard 'agent = computer + email + phone', '$12/hr' circled, then a two-week hours-saved tally, caption 'sell the hours back'.

virals.draft_en:
The biggest AI research post this week: researchers say GPT-6 Astra edited a small Qwen model's weights directly, changing only 0.016% of them, and improved its math up to 6x without any training. 7.5M views, 34k bookmarks.

Within hours, others built on it. One person ran a Writing Weights Index showing open-source models struggle at the task. Simon Willison tried the idea on a local model.

It's early and the claims come from the authors, so wait for replications. But the builder lesson is already clear: the day a big result lands, a small tool or test on top of it gets attention.
virals.inspired_by: @rikiyatakehi weight-space programming (7.55M, 34k bookmarks) + @xingyudang Writing Weights Index (282k) + @simonw local test (16k) + @yoheinakajima viral projects (7k) + @tdinh_me 'superhuman' (5k)
virals.video_tip: 10s: weight grid with a few cells changing, then '0.016% edited, math up to 6x (authors' claim)', caption 'test it before you trust it'.

virals.angle: Agents on the server, with guardrails
virals.draft_en:
Tony Dinh's new habit: the first thing he installs on any server he SSHs into is Claude Code.

At the same time, Goldman Sachs is reportedly pulling Claude Code back to engineers only, and Amjad Masad says agents on employee machines are becoming a systemic security risk.

Both can be true. Agents are great on a box if:
1. Ports are closed and access is least privilege
2. Secrets are scoped to that job
3. Anything destructive needs your review

Speed and guardrails, not one or the other.
